diaphragm.nerves: Phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) — "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"
diaphragm.actions: Inspiration; modulates intra-abdominal pressure for trunk stiffness

longissimus thoracis.nerves: Lateral branches of the posterior rami of spinal nerves, segmentally
longissimus thoracis.actions: Trunk and neck extension, ipsilateral lateral flexion, eccentric control of flexion

gluteus maximus.actions: Hip extension, external rotation, upper fibres abduct; stabilises the extended knee via the IT tract

latissimus dorsi.actions: Humeral extension, adduction and medial rotation; assists trunk extension

transversus abdominis.actions: Compresses the abdomen, raises intra-abdominal pressure, tensions thoracolumbar fascia

multifidus.nerves: Medial branches of the posterior rami of spinal nerves, segmentally
multifidus.actions: Segmental stabilisation; small contributions to extension and contralateral rotation

rectus abdominis.actions: Trunk flexion, posterior pelvic tilt, raises intra-abdominal pressure

external oblique.actions: Contralateral rotation, ipsilateral lateral flexion, trunk flexion, posterior pelvic tilt

internal oblique.actions: Ipsilateral rotation and lateral flexion, trunk flexion, abdominal compression

psoas major.nerves: Anterior rami of L1–L3 directly (not via the femoral nerve)
psoas major.actions: Hip flexion, external rotation of hip; with the femur fixed, lumbar flexion and lateral flexion

gluteus medius.actions: Hip abduction; anterior fibres medially rotate, posterior fibres laterally rotate; pelvic stabilisation in single-leg stance

tensor fasciae latae.actions: Hip flexion, abduction and medial rotation; tensions the iliotibial tract

quadratus lumborum.nerves: Subcostal nerve (T12) and anterior rami of L1–L4
quadratus lumborum.actions: Lateral flexion of trunk, elevation of ipsilateral ilium, fixes rib 12

serratus anterior.actions: Scapular protraction and upward rotation; holds the scapula against the thorax

deltoid.actions: Abduction; anterior part flexes and medially rotates, posterior part extends and laterally rotates

triceps brachii.actions: Elbow extension; shoulder extension and adduction from the long head

trapezius.nerves: Accessory nerve (CN XI) for motor; C3–C4 for proprioception
trapezius.actions: Upper: scapular elevation. Middle: retraction. Lower: depression and upward rotation.

gastrocnemius.actions: Plantarflexion of the ankle, assists knee flexion

soleus.actions: Plantarflexion; postural control of forward sway in standing

biceps femoris.nerves: Long head: tibial division of sciatic (L5, S1, S2). Short head: common fibular division (L5, S1, S2).
biceps femoris.actions: Knee flexion, hip extension, lateral rotation of the flexed knee

piriformis.nerves: Nerve to piriformis, from the sacral plexus
piriformis.actions: Hip lateral rotation in extension, abduction in flexion, sacroiliac stabilisation

obturator internus.actions: Hip lateral rotation, abduction of the flexed hip, femoral head centring

semitendinosus.nerves: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2)
semitendinosus.actions: Knee flexion, hip extension, medial rotation of the flexed knee

adductor magnus.nerves: Obturator nerve (adductor part) and tibial division of the sciatic nerve (hamstring part)
adductor magnus.actions: Hip adduction throughout; hip extension from the ischiocondylar part

pubococcygeus.nerves: Nerve to levator ani, with a pudendal contribution
pubococcygeus.actions: Pelvic floor elevation, visceral support, intra-abdominal pressure regulation

semimembranosus.nerves: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve
semimembranosus.actions: Hip extension, knee flexion, medial rotation of the flexed knee

gluteus minimus.actions: Hip abduction, medial rotation, pelvic stabilisation in stance

abductor hallucis.actions: Hallux abduction and flexion, arch elevation

fibularis longus.actions: Ankle eversion and plantarflexion; first ray plantarflexion

neural_strength.claim: The first few weeks of strength training make you stronger by changing the nervous system, before the muscle grows at all.
neural_strength.mechanism: Motor unit discharge rates rise, recruitment thresholds fall, and antagonist co-contraction drops. Measurable hypertrophy lags weeks behind the strength gain.
neural_strength.citation: Moritani T, deVries HA, Am J Phys Med 1979;58(3):115–30; Del Vecchio A et al., J Physiol 2019;597(7):1873–87
neural_strength.effect: Most of the strength gain in weeks 1–4 is neural; hypertrophy contributes measurably from around week 4–6
neural_strength.caveat: The classic time course comes from small samples and indirect EMG measures; modern high-density EMG supports the direction while revising the details. The crossover point depends on the person and the programme.

apa_timing.claim: In healthy people the deep trunk muscles fire before the limb that is about to move — and that timing is delayed in recurrent low back pain.
apa_timing.mechanism: The nervous system predicts the postural disturbance a movement is about to cause and pre-stiffens the trunk. It is feedforward control, issued before any sensory feedback could arrive.
apa_timing.citation: Hodges PW, Richardson CA, Spine 1996;21(22):2640–50; Exp Brain Res 1997;114:362–70
apa_timing.effect: Transversus abdominis leads the prime mover by roughly 30 ms; in low back pain the lead is lost or reversed
apa_timing.population: Small laboratory samples of adults with and without low back pain
apa_timing.caveat: This is the single best entry point for the Pilates story and also the most over-sold. The original bilateral-brace reading has been contested: Allison and colleagues (2008) showed the response is side-specific and direction-specific, not a uniform corset. And a delayed onset is an association with pain, not a demonstrated cause of it — training the timing has not reliably outperformed general exercise in trials.

motor_learning.claim: Learning a movement moves through distinct stages and distinct structures: fast within-session gains, then slow consolidation across days and sleep.
motor_learning.mechanism: Prefrontal and premotor areas dominate early while the movement is still being figured out; with practice the representation shifts toward primary motor cortex, cerebellum for error correction, and basal ganglia for chunking a sequence into one unit.
motor_learning.citation: Dayan E, Cohen LG, Neuron 2011;72(3):443–54 (review); Doyon J, Benali H, Curr Opin Neurobiol 2005;15(2):161–7
motor_learning.population: Healthy adults, motor sequence and adaptation paradigms
motor_learning.caveat: The staged account comes largely from finger-sequence and reaching tasks in a scanner. Whole-body movement under load is not the same problem, and the mapping to a Pilates repertoire is an extrapolation.

external_focus.claim: Directing attention outside the body — to the effect of the movement — produces better performance and better retention than directing it at the body part.
external_focus.mechanism: The constrained action hypothesis: attending to your own limb interferes with automatic control processes that run better without conscious supervision.
external_focus.citation: Chua L-K et al., Psychol Bull 2021;147(6):618–45 (meta-analysis, 218 studies); Wulf G, Int Rev Sport Exerc Psychol 2013;6(1):77–104
external_focus.effect: Small-to-moderate advantage for external focus across accuracy, force production and retention
external_focus.population: Mostly healthy adults, laboratory and sport tasks
external_focus.caveat: This sits in real tension with how Pilates is traditionally taught — "draw your navel to your spine" is an internal cue, and the tradition is built on them. The honest position is that the evidence favours external cues for performance while internal cues may still be useful for teaching a person to find a muscle they cannot yet feel. This app surfaces the tension rather than resolving it.

interoception_breath.claim: Attending to the breath engages the insula and anterior cingulate, and nasal breathing entrains oscillations in limbic structures.
interoception_breath.mechanism: The insula is the cortical destination for signals from inside the body. Airflow through the nose rhythmically drives piriform cortex, amygdala and hippocampus in phase with the breath.
interoception_breath.citation: Zelano C et al., J Neurosci 2016;36(49):12448–67 (7 patients with intracranial electrodes); Critchley HD et al., Nat Neurosci 2004;7(2):189–95
interoception_breath.effect: Breath-locked oscillatory entrainment; behavioural effects on fear discrimination and recall were small and nasal-specific
interoception_breath.population: Seven epilepsy patients with implanted electrodes, plus healthy behavioural samples
interoception_breath.caveat: Seven patients. This is the finding most likely to be inflated into "breathwork rewires your brain", and it does not support that. Pilates lateral costal breathing has no direct imaging evidence at all — the link from this work to that practice is inference.

balance_cerebellum.claim: Balance and coordination training changes cerebellar and cortical grey matter, and improves postural control in older adults.
balance_cerebellum.mechanism: The cerebellum computes the error between the movement predicted and the movement that happened. Training that repeatedly generates and corrects that error is training the structure that does the correcting.
balance_cerebellum.citation: Taubert M et al., J Neurosci 2010;30(35):11670–7; Lesinski M et al., Sports Med 2015;45(12):1721–38 (meta-analysis, balance training in older adults)
balance_cerebellum.effect: Moderate-to-large improvement in static and dynamic balance measures in older adults
balance_cerebellum.population: Healthy adults; the balance meta-analysis is specifically older adults
balance_cerebellum.caveat: Structural MRI changes over weeks are small and their functional meaning is debated. The balance improvement is solid; the grey-matter story attached to it is much softer.

slow_breathing_hrv.claim: Breathing slowly, at around six breaths a minute, raises heart rate variability and shifts autonomic balance toward the parasympathetic side while it is happening.
slow_breathing_hrv.mechanism: At roughly 0.1 Hz the breathing rhythm resonates with the baroreflex, so blood pressure oscillations and respiratory sinus arrhythmia line up and amplify each other. Vagal outflow to the heart rises with it.
slow_breathing_hrv.citation: Lehrer PM, Gevirtz R, Front Psychol 2014;5:756; Laborde S et al., Neurosci Biobehav Rev 2022;138:104711 (meta-analysis of slow-paced breathing)
slow_breathing_hrv.effect: Moderate increase in vagally-mediated HRV during and shortly after paced breathing (g ≈ 0.5)
slow_breathing_hrv.population: Healthy adults across many small trials
slow_breathing_hrv.caveat: This is a state, not a trait: the effect is largest while you are breathing that way and shrinks afterwards. Higher HRV during a practice is not evidence that the practice made you a calmer person, and HRV itself is a noisy proxy for "vagal tone" rather than a measurement of it.

stretch_tolerance.claim: Most of the range of motion gained from stretching is increased tolerance to the sensation, not a longer muscle.
stretch_tolerance.mechanism: Passive torque at a given joint angle changes little over weeks of stretching, while the angle at which the stretch becomes intolerable moves. The change is in how the nervous system interprets and permits the position.
stretch_tolerance.citation: Weppler CH, Magnusson SP, Phys Ther 2010;90(3):438–49; Freitas SR et al., Scand J Med Sci Sports 2018;28(3):794–806 (systematic review)
stretch_tolerance.effect: Range increases substantially; passive stiffness at matched angles changes little over programmes under about eight weeks
stretch_tolerance.population: Healthy adults, mostly hamstring and calf protocols
stretch_tolerance.caveat: It does not mean tissue never adapts — longer, heavier or loaded protocols do change muscle architecture. It means the fast gains a class produces are a nervous-system change, and describing them as "lengthening the muscle" is describing the wrong organ.

tiers.B: One human RCT, or consistent observational evidence
tiers.C: Human mechanistic or imaging work, small samples
tiers.E: Mechanistic inference — reasoning, not a finding
